units: the writer is addressing her neighbour about their two flats

the writer is watching a crack widen behind a radiator
the two neighbours air their flats in opposite ways
the writer suggests calling in a tradesman for both levels
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing to you about our two flats, which turn out to need rather different care. Yours sits directly beneath the roof, so the tiles pass their heat straight down to you, and you close the wooden shutter on the landing well before noon. Mine takes up the lowest level of the house, where a cold damp lifts the wallpaper away from the skirting board. You fight dry air; I fight wet walls. You wipe away the fine grit that drifts in through the gaps in the roof timbers, while I keep an eye on a thin crack widening behind the radiator. Even our remedies pull in opposite directions: you throw a window open for a few minutes, whereas I have to warm the room first. Might I suggest that we call in a tradesman together, so that he can look over both levels on one visit?

units: delicate laundry is best washed by hand
the water should be lukewarm and the soak short
a small amount of soap saves repeated rinsing
the fabric must not be wrung out hard
a dry towel serves to draw off the water held in the cloth
drying is done flat and away from a source of heat
stretching the damp garment does away with ironing
an old stain is soaked before any wash
boiling water would set the colour of the stain
text: Should delicate laundry be washed by hand? In most cases, yes. Lukewarm water and a short soak are kinder to the fibres than a drum spinning at full speed. How much soap? Very little. Too much lather leaves you rinsing the load twice or three times over. Should you wring it out hard? Never. Press the fabric between your palms instead, then roll it in a dry towel to draw off the water it still holds. Where should it dry? Flat, well away from any direct source of heat, on a surface that lets air move underneath. And the ironing? You can skip that altogether if you stretch the garment while it is still damp and set the crease with your fingers. What about an old stain? Soak it before any wash, and keep it clear of boiling water, which would set the colour rather than lift it.

units: the caretaker asks the narrator about noises in the night

text: The caretaker stopped me in the entrance hall and wanted to know whether I had heard anything at all in the night. Not a thing, I told him, for I had slept straight through until morning. He said he had first caught sight of a figure by the letterboxes, and then heard a wooden shutter bang somewhere on the floor above. So down he went with his torch, and there on the mat outside the door at the far end lay a key. Whose was it, I wanted to know. He shrugged and owned that he had no idea at all. A while later the tenant from upstairs turned up to claim it: she had let her door swing shut behind her while taking the bins down, and hadn't the nerve to wake her neighbours. He had a good laugh about that, then told me to leave a spare with somebody I trust. I rather think I shall, this very week.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once depended on a well or a fountain

the coming of indoor pipes altered domestic habits

clothes were changed more often
the making of light fabrics grew
floors could be cleaned with plenty of water
smooth coverings pushed out the bare boards
text: Before piped water reached the home, fetching it governed the whole domestic day. A household depended on a well or a public fountain, and every drop arrived bucket by bucket, up whatever stairs there were. That is why washing was gathered into one great operation a week rather than spread about. When pipes finally ran indoors, far more changed than mere comfort. Water now came without effort, so the wash broke up into smaller and more frequent ones, garments were changed more often, and the making of light fabrics grew to keep pace. A second consequence followed close behind. Floors that had once been swept dry in a cloud of dust could be sluiced with water, and smooth coverings soon pushed out the bare boards. Plumbing, in short, reshaped both the furniture and the clothing.

units: pastry that tears puts beginners off

shaking the flour through a sieve lets air into it

grating the butter scatters it in fragments
the fingertips can also crumble it

a rest in the cold under a damp cloth slackens the mixture
text: Pastry that tears under the rolling pin has put many a beginner off for good. The fault seldom lies with the hands. It begins in the flour, which packs itself into tight little lumps as soon as it has sat a while in its bag. The cure is an old gesture: shake it through a sieve above the bowl, so that air passes through it and lightens it. Butter raises a kindred difficulty. Straight from the cold it is a solid block, and no pastry will take a fat as hard as that. Grate it, then, on the coarse side of a grater, or crumble it between your fingertips until it lies scattered in tiny flakes. Last comes the question of rest. Worked too briskly, pastry shrinks back in the heat and leaves ragged edges; left cool beneath a damp cloth, it slackens, settles, and rolls out with surprising ease.

units: the craftsman sets out two tubes of glue for the narrator

the second glue sets on contact with the moisture in the air
the second glue grips very quickly

the joint made by the second snaps under a twist
the craftsman keeps the slow glue for the load-bearing piece
a thick layer of glue holds less well than a thin film
text: The joiner who came to mend the shelf laid two tubes of glue side by side and told me they did not work alike. The first is water-based: it soaks into the grain and hardens as the water leaves it, which means a long spell in the clamps and a room that is not cold. The second sets on contact with the moisture in the air, grips within moments, and takes to smooth surfaces such as metal or ceramic. You pay for that speed elsewhere. The first leaves a joint with some give in it, one that follows the seasonal swelling of the wood, whereas the second forms a rigid edge that snaps clean under a twist. So he kept the slow one for the load-bearing rail and the quick one for the decorative beading. The commonest error, he added, is to lay it on thick: a heavy film gives way before the fibres it joins.

units: the wardrobe must be emptied altogether before starting

text: Storing clothes away from one season to the next repays a settled order. Begin by emptying the wardrobe altogether, wipe the shelves down with a damp cloth, and leave the surfaces to dry in the open air. Next, sort the garments into three groups: those you still wear, those that stand in need of mending, and those you will part with. Then wash everything you mean to keep, even what appears perfectly clean, since an unseen trace of sweat will draw moths during storage. Fold each piece flat rather than hanging it up, which spares the shoulders from stretching out of shape. Slip a sachet of scented wood in between the layers, and never anything liquid. Finally, write on a label what every box holds, and set the heaviest of them at the bottom of the stack, where they will not crush the rest.

text: The main gave way shortly before daybreak, in the street that runs alongside the covered market. Residents were the first to report a warm puddle spreading at the foot of a lamp post; then the paving lifted and the water reached the cellars of the buildings nearby. A standby crew arrived before the shops had opened and shut off the supply to the whole quarter. The traders shifted their stalls to the hall close by, where two taps were still running. By the middle of the afternoon the technicians had cleared the broken iron and found that a root had worked an old joint loose. The repair was finished after dark, yet the water stayed cloudy for a whole evening, and the service told residents to run it off before using it for food. Pumps will drain the flooded cellars in the course of next week.

units: the house described belongs to the narrator's uncle

text: Walk into my uncle's house and you see at once that it was built with its back to the wind. The front door gives onto a narrow passage, because whoever put it up wanted the heat held close to the hearth. That is why the kitchen is the largest room and swallows all the traffic: people eat there, mend their bicycles there, hang up soaked coats to dry there. The walls carry a dull green that came from the last of a tin; there was not enough of it, so the upper part stayed a good deal paler. The tiled floor slopes towards the garden door, an old trick for letting the washing water run out, which is why the children's marbles all roll the same way. And since the far window looks onto a blank wall, my uncle hung a mirror opposite, to throw a little light back onto the table where the family gathers of an evening.

the writer asks landlords to set aside a room for such exchanges
text: Our homes fill up with things that we use for one season only, and tidying them has become an occupation in its own right. The trouble is not that we own a great deal of it; it is that nothing circulates. A machine bought for one particular dish sleeps in a cupboard while a neighbour hunts about for the very same thing. No moral appeal to own less is going to mend that. What will mend it are quiet arrangements that make borrowing as easy as buying. Tool stores already exist in some blocks of flats, run by the tenants themselves, who write each loan down in a notebook. Where they work, they rest on three rules: a modest deposit, a short loan, and repairs shared out among the borrowers. Landlords ought to set aside a room for such exchanges, just as they set one aside for prams.
